title: Sound Resonance in Pipes (open–closed)
theory: Closed end (piston) = displacement node; open end ≈ displacement antinode. An open–closed column of length $L$ resonates when $L = (2k-1)\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$, $k = 1, 2, 3, \dots$ — odd quarter-wavelengths only — giving frequencies $f_k = (2k-1)\dfrac{V}{4L}$ (**odd harmonics only**). Successive resonance *positions* at fixed frequency are spaced $\lambda/2$, which conveniently cancels the end correction. (Open–open pipes: $L = k\lambda/2$, all harmonics.)
framework: Use the $\lambda/2$ spacing between resonances as the robust measurement.

parts.title: Wavelength
parts.parameters:
- Given: horizontal tube, open at the left where a speaker of frequency $f$ plays; a movable piston closes it at distance $x$ from the opening; loud sound (resonance) occurs first at $x = l$ and next at $x = 3l$.
- Find: $\lambda$; the speed of sound; the interior point of maximum density variation at the second resonance; how $l$ shifts on a hot day; the next resonance frequency with the piston fixed at $3l$.
- Diagram: speaker | ←— air column of length $x$ —→ | piston.

parts.title: Speed of sound
parts.parameters:
- Given: horizontal tube, open at the left where a speaker of frequency $f$ plays; a movable piston closes it at distance $x$ from the opening; loud sound (resonance) occurs first at $x = l$ and next at $x = 3l$.
- Find: $\lambda$; the speed of sound; the interior point of maximum density variation at the second resonance; how $l$ shifts on a hot day; the next resonance frequency with the piston fixed at $3l$.
- Diagram: speaker | ←— air column of length $x$ —→ | piston.
parts.conclusion: cross-check: resonance spacing $3l - l = 2l$ must equal $\lambda/2$ ✓ — in lab-style questions use the spacing as the primary measurement (end corrections cancel).

parts.title: Maximum density variation at the second resonance
parts.parameters:
- Given: horizontal tube, open at the left where a speaker of frequency $f$ plays; a movable piston closes it at distance $x$ from the opening; loud sound (resonance) occurs first at $x = l$ and next at $x = 3l$.
- Find: $\lambda$; the speed of sound; the interior point of maximum density variation at the second resonance; how $l$ shifts on a hot day; the next resonance frequency with the piston fixed at $3l$.
- Diagram: speaker | ←— air column of length $x$ —→ | piston.
parts.formulas: density variation is maximal at **displacement nodes**: the piston face $x = 3l$ and every $\lambda/2 = 2l$ toward the opening.
parts.conclusion: the open end ($x=0$) is an antinode — zero density variation. Nodes carry the pressure action.

parts.title: Effect of higher air temperature on l
parts.parameters:
- Given: horizontal tube, open at the left where a speaker of frequency $f$ plays; a movable piston closes it at distance $x$ from the opening; loud sound (resonance) occurs first at $x = l$ and next at $x = 3l$.
- Find: $\lambda$; the speed of sound; the interior point of maximum density variation at the second resonance; how $l$ shifts on a hot day; the next resonance frequency with the piston fixed at $3l$.
- Diagram: speaker | ←— air column of length $x$ —→ | piston.
parts.formulas: $V$ increases with temperature ⇒ $\lambda = V/f$ increases ⇒ $l = \lambda/4$ increases.
parts.conclusion: qualitative chain $T\uparrow \Rightarrow V\uparrow \Rightarrow \lambda\uparrow \Rightarrow l\uparrow$ — MEXT loves this one-step inference.

parts.title: Next resonance frequency, piston fixed at L = 3l
parts.parameters:
- Given: horizontal tube, open at the left where a speaker of frequency $f$ plays; a movable piston closes it at distance $x$ from the opening; loud sound (resonance) occurs first at $x = l$ and next at $x = 3l$.
- Find: $\lambda$; the speed of sound; the interior point of maximum density variation at the second resonance; how $l$ shifts on a hot day; the next resonance frequency with the piston fixed at $3l$.
- Diagram: speaker | ←— air column of length $x$ —→ | piston.
parts.calculations: modes: $\frac{f}{3}, f, \frac{5f}{3}, \dots$ — the current resonance is $f$ ($k=2$); the next above it is $\frac{5}{3}f$.
parts.conclusion: only **odd** multiples of $f/3$ exist in an open–closed tube — the step from $f$ is $\frac{2}{3}f$, not $\frac{1}{3}f$, because the even mode does not exist.
